stories.title: China’s netizens rage against professor who said gig work was a type of ‘welfare’
stories.summary: The term “flexible employment” has gone viral in China.
article_sentences: An economics professor called gig work a form of "welfare" due to its flexibility, sparking public anger over job insecurity in China.
The number of flexible workers in China is expected to reach 320 million by 2026, raising concerns about social protection and pension systems.
Critics say the professor's comments ignored gig workers' hardships, while some note her past advocacy for their social security rights.

The term “flexible employment” has gone viral in China after a prominent economics professor described gig work as a form of “welfare”, drawing widespread public anger and highlighting deep anxieties over job insecurity.

Zhang Dandan, a professor of economics and deputy dean at Peking University’s National School of Development, made the remarks during a discussion on social protection for gig workers, on the popular financial show “Let’s Talk” last week.
She argued that from the perspective of labour economics, “flexibility itself is a form of welfare.”
While regular employees trade schedule flexibility for pensions and other benefits, flexible workers enjoy greater control over their time at the cost of weaker social protections, Zhang said.
The comments triggered a fierce backlash over the weekend, with social media users accusing Zhang of being oblivious to the harsh realities of the gig economy.
Zhang did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.
The controversy has struck a nerve for many in China, where a cooling economy has made secure, full-time employment harder to find.

The China New Employment Forms Research Centre, a think tank, estimates the number of flexible workers – those without permanent full-time contracts – will rise to 320 million in 2026 from 280 million in 2025.
That represents about 44 per cent of China’s urban workforce and is roughly equivalent to the entire population of the United States.

stories.title: Thai PM meets security chiefs after coordinated attacks in three southern provinces
stories.summary: As has often been the case with such incidents, no group was immediately publicly blamed or claimed responsibility for the actions.
article_sentences: As has often been the case with such incidents, no group was immediately publicly blamed or claimed responsibility for the actions.

Thailand’s Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul, already facing a flood crisis in the country’s north, held an urgent meeting on Sunday with high-level security officials in response to coordinated violence overnight in three southern provinces where a small-scale Muslim insurgency is active.
The meeting, held shortly before Anutin flew north to inspect the badly flooded province of Nan, followed 51 incidents on Saturday night in the southernmost provinces of Narathiwat, Pattani and Yala.
The attackers did not engage with military or police forces.
Only three civilians were known to have been wounded and they were reported to be recovering on Sunday.
The violence primarily involved small bombs, arson and other forms of property damage.
The highest-profile target was a 7-Eleven convenience store in Pattani.
A video circulating on social media appeared to show armed men stalking outside the store while customers and workers fled before it was set on fire.
A bomb that damaged rail tracks in Narathiwat forced the suspension of local and long-haul services.
It was not clear when they would be restored due to the uncertain security situation.
However, such attacks are generally believed to be carried out by the Barisan Revolusi Nasional Melayu Patani (BRN).
It is the major insurgent group in the south with the organisational means and support to stage such an action.
